newsitem.title: UK: CPI data, EMU, dollar conspire against the mark.
newsitem.headline: CPI data, EMU, dollar conspire against the mark.

text.p: The mark stayed down on the crosses at midday Europe, depressed by a blend of CPI data, cautious EMU optimism and a robust dollar/mark, analysts said.
That provided some relief for the lira, which was knocked on Wednesday by EU forecasts suggesting it and Greece would be the only states failing to qualify for the launch of monetary union.
Economists applauded a 0.1 percent fall in West German preliminary April CPI, which rose 1.4 percent year-on-year.
"These are good numbers -- the Bundesbank can't be at all worried with those sort of numbers," said Elizabeth Legge, chief economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin in London.

"(The figures) mean the Bundesbank's got a certain amount of scope, but I don't think it'll change its monetary stance," said Legge. Other factors, such as faith in a German and general European pick-up, should stay the bank's hand, she added.
Germany's six top economic research institutes predicted this week that the Bundesbank would hold interest rates steady this year but tighten policy slightly in early 1998.
The mark was trading at 992.65/3.05 lire and 3.3714/19 French francs at 1010 GMT, down from late Wednesday's European levels of 995.20/30 and 3.3734/39 respectively.

The fact that the European Union's spring forecasts released yesterday had foreseen all but two states meeting EMU criteria had boosted market optimism the project would proceed as planned and consequently weighed on the mark, analysts said.
"The EU forecasts were broadly speaking encouraging for EMU prospects in 1999, and that's contributed (to a softer mark)," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered here.

The market shrugged off International Monetary Fund warnings that not only Italy, but also EMU-lynchpins Germany and France could overshoot the Maastricht target of a 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP ratio.

Though the IMF forecasts were perhaps more credible since they were more objective than those of the European Commission, the perception that the ultimate decision on EMU participation would be political meant the market had concentrated on the EU's predictions, analysts said.
The approach of this weekend's Group of Seven meeting also dragged on the mark, analysts noted. The market believes the strength of dollar/yen, and not dollar/mark, is likely to preoccupy the G7.
